comments.original: Zhanhong He has provided a PhD thesis which consists of 154 pages, 127 of which make up the main body of the text which consists of seven chapters. The core methodological chapters are chapters 3-6, with the first two providing an introduction and background and the last chapter being the thesis conclusions. Overall the document is well written and clearly organised, with no comments on the overall chapter structure. In terms of citation style, I would suggest to use an author-year format which improves readability given a lack of space constraints. The use of language and the overall presentation of the text is excellent. In general the thesis is of high quality and was a pleasure to read.

locations.before: Music performance is commonly represented in two complementary symbolic forms. The first is MIDI, where note events are paired with note-level expressive parameters such as velocity. MIDI velocity is precise, machine-readable, and often comes from the sensor measurements in musical instruments. The second is the music score, where dynamics is represented by human-readable markings such as \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, \textit{ff}. These markings are relative, context-dependent, and less precise as physical measurements, but they communicate musical intent on a musically meaningful metrical grid.
locations.after: This thesis posits that dynamics is a foundational component of expressive AMT. While music expression is multifaceted, dynamics represents the most perceptually salient and practically essential dimension. Unlike a standard transcription that yields flat intensities, a dynamics-aware approach enables expressive rendering and high-quality symbolic corpora curation. By focusing on the robust recovery of score dynamics and MIDI velocity, this work provides a critical layer of musical information.

\section{Unified Thesis Question and Three Core Scenarios}
\label{sec:intro:question}
locations.after:
This question is studied under three core scenarios, outlined in Table~\ref{tab:intro_scenarios}. These scenarios represent a clear methodological progression. \textbf{Scenario S1} isolates the recovery task to a strict \textit{symbolic-only} setting. \textbf{Scenario S2} introduces acoustic evidence but maintains a reliable structural prior via an \textit{audio-plus-score} alignment. Finally, \textbf{Scenario S3} removes structural support entirely, tackling the fully open, \textit{audio-only} setting to recover a \textit{score-facing} target. By intentionally ordering these environments from the tightly constrained to the ambiguous, they form the core empirical arc of the thesis.

locations.quote: From the thesis perspective, this chapter occupies a distinct position. It keeps the note-level MIDI velocity target and the score-informed VeloEst architecture introduced in Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf}, but it relaxes the assumption that ground-truth velocity labels are available for the target instrument. It complements Chapter~\ref{ch:audiodyn}, which addressed Scenario~S3 with a different output (beat-synchronous score dynamics), by extending the velocity-focused work to a label-scarce setting. The chapter therefore contributes to thesis Requirement~R5 by combining numerical diagnostics, perceptual loudness correlations, and renderer-robust evaluation evidence, and to Requirement~R6 by treating beyond-piano transfer as a missing-supervision problem rather than ordinary acoustic domain shift.
locations.before: This framing leads to two candidate supervision interfaces. The first is a differentiable waveform synthesiser (Diff-Synth) that renders predicted velocities into audio and matches them against the real recording in waveform or spectral space. The second is a differentiable SoundFont proxy (Diff-SFProxy) that maps predicted velocities to note-wise loudness-related acoustic parameters and matches those parameters against measurements of the real audio. Both interfaces share the same front-end estimator and the same regularisers, so the comparison isolates the effect of the supervision signal itself.
locations.after: The chapter is delimited in two respects. First, label-scarce cross-instrument velocity estimation has few direct baselines that target the same setting. Second, renderer-based supervision introduces a renderer-conditioned interpretation of velocity that does not coincide with a single physical measurement of the performer's gesture. The chapter is therefore framed as a practical solution under explicit assumptions, rather than as a claim about universal real-performance fidelity.

locations.quote: VeloEst acts as the shared front-end of the framework, estimating note-wise MIDI velocities $\hat{V}$ from the performance audio and aligned note events. We use the score-informed HPT model with onset and frame as score-guidance, which is identified as the best VeloEst configuration in Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf}~\cite{he2026score}. We keep its architecture unchanged and use the publicly available checkpoint trained on MAESTRO with ground-truth velocity supervision $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{velo}}$. This fixed estimator keeps the cross-instrument experiment focused on the supervision interface rather than on introducing a new velocity-estimation architecture.
locations.before:
\subsection{VeloEst: Shared Front-End Estimator}
\label{ssec:bp:veloest}
locations.after: The estimator has two stages. The acoustic module, borrowed from the High-Resolution Piano Transcription system~\cite{kong2021hpt}, takes log-Mel spectrograms computed at $100$\,fps from $22050$\,Hz mono audio (FFT size $2048$, hop $221$\,samples, Hann window) as input and predicts a coarse velocity roll $V^{(0)}$. A score-informed Transformer then refines $V^{(0)}$ into $\hat{V}$ using aligned note information. The detailed architecture and supervised training procedure are given in Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf}; the present chapter treats this estimator as a fixed black-box front-end whose checkpoint is then adapted.

locations.quote:
The word \emph{velocity} is often described informally as key-strike force. For keyboard instruments this is useful but imprecise. In sensor-equipped acoustic pianos, the recorded value is more accurately treated as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion near the note attack. Studies of computer-controlled pianos distinguish the player's physical action, the hammer--string interaction, the measured control value, and the resulting acoustic signal \cite{goebl2003role,goebl2004piano}. Large piano datasets such as MAESTRO use this property to provide aligned audio and MIDI data with key-strike velocity labels, making note-level velocity a practical target for MIR systems \cite{hawthorne2019maestro}.

MIDI velocity is exact as symbolic data. A note with velocity 80 remains velocity 80 when the MIDI file is copied, edited, or passed to a model. It is also mechanical in the sense that it refers to a local performance control: how strongly a note attack is executed or how strongly a synthesiser should respond. This objectivity is one reason why velocity is attractive for automatic transcription, expressive rendering, and symbolic performance modelling \cite{ewert2011est,kim2023score,kim2024method}.

However, exactness in the data structure does not imply universality in sound. MIDI velocity is not loudness, not amplitude, and not a dynamic marking. It is a control parameter whose acoustic effect depends on the instrument, renderer, register, sample layer, synthesis design, and recording chain. Dannenberg's analysis of MIDI velocity shows that different synthesisers and patches implement substantially different velocity-response curves \cite{dan2006psy}. Thus, a MIDI value can be objective without being perceptually absolute. It is exact as a note-level control value, but relative as an acoustic and musical quantity.

In conventional MIDI performance data, a sounding note onset carries a discrete velocity value on a finite integer scale. In a chord, each note may have a different velocity. The word \emph{velocity} is often described informally as key-strike force. For keyboard instruments this is useful but imprecise. In sensor-equipped acoustic pianos, the recorded value is more accurately treated as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion near the note attack. Studies of computer-controlled pianos distinguish the player's physical action, the hammer--string interaction, the measured control value, and the resulting acoustic signal \cite{goebl2003role,goebl2004piano}. Large piano datasets such as MAESTRO use this property to provide aligned audio and MIDI data with key-strike velocity labels, making note-level velocity a practical target for MIR systems \cite{hawthorne2019maestro}.

MIDI velocity is exact as symbolic data. A note with velocity 80 remains velocity 80 when the MIDI file is copied, edited, or passed to a model. It is also mechanical in the sense that it refers to a local performance control: how strongly a note attack is executed or how strongly a synthesiser should respond. This objectivity is one reason why velocity is attractive for automatic transcription, expressive rendering, and symbolic performance modelling \cite{ewert2011est,kim2023score,kim2024method}.

However, exactness in the data structure does not imply universality in sound. MIDI velocity is not loudness, not amplitude, and not a dynamic marking. It is a control parameter whose acoustic effect depends on the instrument, renderer, register, sample layer, synthesis design, and recording chain. Dannenberg's analysis of MIDI velocity shows that different synthesisers and patches implement substantially different velocity-response curves \cite{dan2006psy}. Thus, a MIDI value can be objective without being perceptually absolute. It is exact as a note-level control value, but relative as an acoustic and musical quantity.

\paragraph{Score dynamics.}
Score dynamics represents the subjective cognitive intention of the composer or performer. Instead of attaching to isolated notes, markings like \textit{p} or \textit{crescendo} are conceptually anchored to the underlying metrical structure, acting as shared values across a specific beat or an entire phrase. This section identifies a narrower and more practical research gap than the general claim that AMT still lacks expressiveness. A recurring paradox in music research is that while structural data (pitch and timing) is increasingly abundant, expressive data remains systematically impoverished. A MIDI file may contain correct note sequences while leaving all velocities at a default constant. A performance corpus may preserve audio and aligned scores but only sparse, unreliable, or absent dynamic markings. The common problem is therefore how to recover a missing expressive label layer from data that are already partly specified.

\paragraph{The ontological gap: dynamics must be inferred across representations.}
locations.after:
\paragraph{The ambiguity of ground truth: dynamics is more fragile than notes.}
For note transcription, pitch and onset often remain learnable under moderate changes in instrument, room, or recording conditions. Dynamics ground truth is less stable. Small changes in instruments (timbre), microphone placement, editorial convention, or synthesis setup can alter the apparent relation between sound, MIDI velocity, and score dynamics notation. For non-piano settings, the difficulty becomes sharper because the bottleneck is not ordinary domain shift but missing measurement itself: reliable MIDI velocity labels are rarely available, and in some cases even the ground truth is instrument-dependent.

Expressive performance rendering aims to generate expressive control signals from symbolic input. Many systems predict timing, dynamics, and sometimes articulation jointly \cite{jeong2019virtuosonet,borovik2023scoreperformer}. These models are important because they show that expressive performance can be learned from symbolic structure. At the same time, they reveal a practical limitation for the present thesis. Joint expressive rendering may alter more than the user wants. This narrower, controllable objective is the entry point for Chapter~\ref{ch:velcomp}.

locations.quote: Dynamic markings are the conventional score vocabulary for notated loudness and dynamic change. They include static markings such as \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mp}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}, as well as directional indications such as \textit{crescendo}, \textit{diminuendo}, and hairpins. Although a marking is printed at a specific visual position, its musical scope is usually broader than that position. A single \textit{p} may govern a phrase, a texture, or a formal region until a later marking or musical event changes the dynamic state. A crescendo indicates a tendency over a span, not an isolated value at one note.
locations.before:
\subsection{Dynamic markings as macro-level musical instructions}
\label{sec:bg:dynamic_markings}
locations.after: The crucial point is that dynamic markings are not calibrated volume labels. They are relational instructions. A \textit{forte} passage is not defined by a fixed sound-pressure level, nor does a \textit{piano} passage prescribe a fixed physical intensity. The intended realisation depends on register, texture, melodic role, harmonic tension, instrumentation, acoustic setting, historical style, and the performer's interpretive priorities. A melody marked \textit{p} may require more acoustic energy than an accompaniment marked \textit{mf}; an inner voice may remain physically soft while sounding perceptually salient because of register or timbral contrast. This context dependence is central to empirical work on the relation between dynamic markings and performed loudness \cite{kosta2014dynpiano,kosta2016mapping}.

alternative_locations_evidence.anchorExact: From a machine-learning perspective, score-dynamics recovery can be framed as classification or structured sequence labelling. The input is audio. The output is a sequence of dynamic symbols or dynamic regimes. The choice of audio representation is therefore not neutral. In the MazurkaBL line of work, the performed-loudness side of this mapping is extracted through sone-based psychoacoustic processing rather than raw amplitude, precisely because the target concerns perceived intensity rather than unweighted energy \cite{kosta2017thesis}. More generally, perceptual front-ends such as Bark-scale specific loudness preserve both a scalar loudness trajectory and the Bark-wise distribution of loudness across the spectrum, which gives a better inductive bias for loudness-oriented tasks than log-Mel features \cite{narang2024automatic,he2026dynest}. Figure~\ref{fig:bg_temporal_units}(a)--(c) shows this contrast on the same excerpt. The practical consequence is also clear: a Nyquist-constrained Bark front-end is substantially lower-dimensional than a $128$-band log-Mel representation, which enables longer audio segments and the phrase-level context that score dynamics actually requires. The challenge is that the labels themselves are sparse, relative, and musically contextual rather than physically absolute. This is one reason why a beat-synchronous formulation is more natural than direct frame-wise regression of continuous loudness.

F1 score is common because the class distribution is imbalanced and because some symbols occur much less frequently than others \cite{kosta2017thesis}. In the present thesis, beat-synchronous evaluation is especially important because it avoids arbitrary frame-level tolerance choices and aligns the prediction target with how the annotations are actually used in music notation.
audit.proposedEnglish: For a given class or event type, precision is TP/(TP+FP), recall is TP/(TP+FN), and F1 is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), where TP, FP, and FN are true positives, false positives, and false negatives. Macro-F1 averages the class-wise scores equally, whereas support-weighted F1 weights them by their reference counts. These averages answer different questions and must be identified when reporting score-dynamics results. Note-level velocity MAE averages the absolute prediction error over the reference note onsets; its full definition and the complementary dispersion metrics are given in Section 3.6.3.

locations.before: For beat and downbeat tracking, the evaluation is event-based rather than frame-based. In other words, beats and downbeats are treated as binary time-stamped events, not as continuous labelled regions. We therefore count matches by one-to-one event alignment: a predicted beat or downbeat is a true positive only if it can be matched to an unmatched reference event within a $\pm 70$~ms window; otherwise it is a false positive, and any unmatched reference event becomes a false negative. We keep this $\pm 70$~ms tolerance because it is the standard F1 setting used by recent beat-tracking work and by \texttt{mir\_eval}, which makes the present results directly comparable with the literature \cite{raffel2014mireval,bock2020deconstruct,foscarin2024beat}. It should therefore be read as an evaluation convention rather than a musically fundamental constant.
locations.after: For change points, the predicted times are first snapped to the nearest ground-truth beat before evaluation. The task then reduces to binary classification on beat indices: a predicted change point is counted as correct only if its snapped beat index exactly matches a reference change-point index. Since both dynamics and change points are evaluated on the same beat grid as the annotations, no additional timing tolerance is required for these two tasks.

These averages answer different questions and must be identified when reporting score-dynamics results. Note-level velocity MAE averages the absolute prediction error over the reference note onsets; its full definition and the complementary dispersion metrics are given in Section 3.6.3.

authorReply.text:
That's a great question, During my Dolby internship, we explored using style as a control parameter in a generative system. Composer could also be used as a coarse style label, for example “Chopin style” or “Beethoven style.”
However, we were facing the data limitation, we don't have enough training data for composer/style control. So we changed our idea from " style control", to make a model can generalize to more data in different style. 
You can see our human listening test analyse the "most-seen composer / unseen composer style" in train data, it exist a gap, but work well across those scenario.s.

\begin{abstract}
	Automatic music transcription has matured in its treatment of note pitch and timing, but musical dynamics remains less fully addressed. This thesis treats dynamics as a missing expressive label layer that can be recovered from music data already partly specified, without rewriting note content or note timing. Its unifying question is \emph{how musically interpretable dynamics labels can be recovered from incomplete, weakly expressive, or weakly supervised music data}. Two complementary targets within expressive music performance recur throughout: note-level MIDI velocity, the per-onset control variable used in MIDI workflows, and score-level dynamics, the beat-aligned markings such as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, and \textit{f} written in notation.
locations.after: It then turns to score-informed velocity estimation in the audio-plus-score setting, using a Transformer correction module that refines AMT-estimated velocity at aligned score onsets. Rather than replacing the AMT backbone, the module uses score structure as a late correction prior, transfers across the HPT, HPPNet, and DynEst backbones, improves cross-dataset behaviour from MAESTRO to SMD, and remains stable under audio--score timing shifts of up to several seconds.

comments.title: image-based和colourisation是否误导读者？
comments.original: Section 3.2 and beyond considers the proposed work as “image-based”. Although there are some related figures with varying colours included in this chapter, I do not see any strong argument for using this term – the methodology does not treat dynamics as a colour channel or similar.
comments.meaning: image-based和colourisation是否误导读者？

authorReply.text:
Good question. The idea originally came from image-processing papers, especially the use of U-Net and window attention. We use “image-based” because both the input and output are two-dimensional pitch–time matrices, processed with two-dimensional convolutions.

The input is a binary piano roll, and the output is a single-channel velocity roll. We do not predict RGB colours. “Colourisation” is an analogy for adding velocity values to the existing note structure, it's good for general audiance understand, but I agree that the wording needs clarification.

I would say the “image-like” is more proper. I will make revision.

locations.before:
\begin{abstract}
	Automatic music transcription has matured in its treatment of note pitch and timing, but musical dynamics remains less fully addressed. This thesis treats dynamics as a missing expressive label layer that can be recovered from music data already partly specified, without rewriting note content or note timing. Its unifying question is \emph{how musically interpretable dynamics labels can be recovered from incomplete, weakly expressive, or weakly supervised music data}. Two complementary targets within expressive music performance recur throughout: note-level MIDI velocity, the per-onset control variable used in MIDI workflows, and score-level dynamics, the beat-aligned markings such as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, and \textit{f} written in notation.
locations.after: It then turns to score-informed velocity estimation in the audio-plus-score setting, using a Transformer correction module that refines AMT-estimated velocity at aligned score onsets. Rather than replacing the AMT backbone, the module uses score structure as a late correction prior, transfers across the HPT, HPPNet, and DynEst backbones, improves cross-dataset behaviour from MAESTRO to SMD, and remains stable under audio--score timing shifts of up to several seconds.

locations.before: Recent symbolic velocity-prediction methods have typically treated the task as sequential prediction. Representative examples include convolutional autoencoders and sequence-to-sequence models with attention \cite{kuo2021velocity,kim2023piano}. These models establish that note-level velocity can be learned from symbolic context. However, piano-roll data is sparse and polyphonic. The relevant structure is not only sequential. It is also spatial. Simultaneous notes create meaningful vertical patterns, and short local pitch--time neighborhoods often carry clear expressive cues.

To process MIDI as images, we convert each performance into three matrices of size \(T \times P\), where \(T\) is the number of time frames and \(P=88\) is the number of piano pitches.
The three matrices are a binary onset roll \(O\), marking note starts; a binary frame roll \(F\), indicating note activation over time; and a velocity roll \(V\), acting as the target colour intensity.
In the implemented system, \(F\) is the network input, \(V\) is the prediction target, and \(O\) is used for onset masking in the loss.
For the velocity roll, integer values in \([0,127]\) are normalised to \([0,1)\) to match the model output activation range.
During post-processing, the model output is denormalised by scaling and rounding back to integer MIDI velocity.
As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:velcomp_model}, these matrices are highly sparse.

locations.quote:
To process MIDI as images, we convert each performance into three matrices of size \(T \times P\), where \(T\) is the number of time frames and \(P=88\) is the number of piano pitches.
The three matrices are a binary onset roll \(O\), marking note starts; a binary frame roll \(F\), indicating note activation over time; and a velocity roll \(V\), acting as the target colour intensity.
In the implemented system, \(F\) is the network input, \(V\) is the prediction target, and \(O\) is used for onset masking in the loss.
For the velocity roll, integer values in \([0,127]\) are normalised to \([0,1)\) to match the model output activation range.
During post-processing, the model output is denormalised by scaling and rounding back to integer MIDI velocity.
As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:velcomp_model}, these matrices are highly sparse.

\paragraph{Procedure.}
Participants were instructed to use headphones because the relevant velocity differences are subtle and are easier to judge at adequate playback quality and level.
In each trial, the audio rendered from the human-performed MIDI served as the fixed reference, and the rendered system outputs were judged relative to that reference.
Following a MUSHRA-inspired reference-based procedure \cite{series2014mursha}, participants rated each processed stimulus independently on a continuous 0--5 scale, where the labelled intervals corresponded to ``bad'', ``poor'', ``fair'', ``good'', and ``excellent'' similarity.
The final scores were averaged across listeners to obtain MOS, and 95\% confidence intervals were computed for reporting.

locations.before: The interface of the proposed system is intentionally simple. The AMT backbone first predicts a preliminary velocity map from audio. The aligned score is then converted into symbolic features at the same time resolution. A lightweight score-informed module finally corrects the preliminary estimate at note onsets. Second, it allows the correction module to be attached to several AMT backbones with only small engineering changes. Third, it constrains the score-informed stage to a narrow task. locations.quote: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.
locations.before: Chapter~\ref{ch:background} already introduced the ambiguity of score dynamics, the distinction between score dynamics and MIDI velocity, and the role of beats and downbeats as a musically meaningful coordinate. Rather than repeat that background, this chapter focuses on the concrete transcription problem studied in this work.
locations.after: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.

locations.quote: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.
locations.before: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.
locations.after: This task directly matches the role assigned to Chapter~5 in the thesis plan: score-level dynamics should be represented as a beat-synchronous interface comprising dynamic levels, change points, and metrical structure. It also supports the broader thesis objective of recovering expressive labels without changing the underlying note content or timing.

locations.quote: Change points are determined in two stages. First, we identify all frames whose change-point probability exceeds 75\%. Second, we snap each candidate to the nearest detected beat. This beat-snapping step is motivated by the annotation style of MazurkaBL, where dynamic markings are beat-aligned rather than freely placed in continuous time \cite{kosta2018mazurkabl}. The step also keeps evaluation consistent with prior work \cite{kosta2017thesis}.
locations.before: The model outputs frame-wise probabilities, which are converted into discrete musical events through tailored post-processing. For beat and downbeat detection, we use the thresholding and local-maximum peak-picking steps of \cite{foscarin2024beat}: probabilities are thresholded at 50\%, and peak picking is applied within a 7-frame local neighbourhood (radius 3 at 50~fps). For dynamic markings, the dynamic level at each beat is determined by taking the \texttt{argmax} of the class probabilities at that frame. When an external beat grid is available, this sampling step is performed on that grid; otherwise, the model's own beat predictions are used, which gives the fully end-to-end mode considered in this chapter.

locations.quote: The 5-fold MazurkaBL evaluation already gives a partial test of generalisation, because the folds are piece-disjoint and the model is always evaluated on unseen mazurkas within the same corpus. However, it remains an in-domain setting: performer pool, recording conditions, repertoire family, and annotation conventions are all inherited from MazurkaBL. We therefore add a stricter cross-dataset experiment on Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart, using them as test-only corpora after the MazurkaBL training stage.
locations.before:
\subsection{Cross-dataset evaluation}
\label{ssec:audiodyn_cross_dataset}
locations.after: For each method and input feature, the five checkpoints obtained from MazurkaBL cross-validation are evaluated on each external corpus without fine-tuning. For multitask systems, the transferred fold is selected by the five-class dynamic F1 score because the dynamic label is the primary output of this chapter; the change-point, beat, and downbeat scores are then reported from the same fold. For single-task systems, each task is trained independently, so the best transferred fold is selected separately for the corresponding task. This mirrors the structure of the in-domain experiments, where the single-task baselines are independent models while the multitask system is a single shared model.

However, it remains an in-domain setting: performer pool, recording conditions, repertoire family, and annotation conventions are all inherited from MazurkaBL. We therefore add a stricter cross-dataset experiment on Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart, using them as test-only corpora after the MazurkaBL training stage.
audit.proposedEnglish: Piece-disjoint cross-validation tests generalisation to unseen mazurkas within MazurkaBL. Cross-dataset evaluation additionally tests the learned mapping under changes in repertoire, performers, recording conditions, and annotation conventions. These factors vary together in Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart, so the experiment diagnoses combined corpus transfer rather than isolating a composer or performer effect.

For multitask systems, the transferred fold is selected by the five-class dynamic F1 score because the dynamic label is the primary output of this chapter; the change-point, beat, and downbeat scores are then reported from the same fold. locations.before: The 5-fold MazurkaBL evaluation already gives a partial test of generalisation, because the folds are piece-disjoint and the model is always evaluated on unseen mazurkas within the same corpus. We therefore add a stricter cross-dataset experiment on Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart, using them as test-only corpora after the MazurkaBL training stage.

locations.quote: Beyond the in-domain MazurkaBL evaluation, Section~\ref{ssec:audiodyn_cross_dataset} reports a test-only cross-dataset evaluation. For each architecture and front-end variant, the five MazurkaBL fold models are all evaluated on Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart without fine-tuning. For the multitask variants, the external table selects the fold with the best dynamic F1 on the target corpus and reports the other task scores from the same checkpoint. For the single-task variants, each task has its own fold models, so the best fold is selected separately for the corresponding task. This protocol is intended as a reproducible transfer diagnostic: it asks whether a MazurkaBL-trained fold checkpoint can be reused on an external classical-piano corpus, while the main MazurkaBL table remains the within-corpus benchmark reported as mean and standard deviation over all folds. The per-fold outputs are retained so that the selected fold can be traced.
locations.before: During training, audio is sliced into 60-second segments with 50\% overlap. No overlap is used at evaluation time. Both BSSL and log-Mel features are extracted with the same STFT configuration to ensure identical temporal resolution. The empirically optimal temporal scaling factor is $s=5$. The model predicts six dynamic classes: one \textit{blank} class and the five annotated dynamic levels \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. On an NVIDIA RTX~3090 (24~GiB), a full 5-fold run requires approximately 20 hours, with peak GPU memory usage around 4~GiB.

locations.quote: The cross-dataset results make this distinction more concrete. If score dynamics were merely a continuous loudness variable relabelled into five fixed bins, an out-of-domain corpus with compatible audio quality would mainly cause smooth calibration errors. Instead, Vienna4x22 shows that the symbolic prior itself matters: a passage that is moderate in acoustic intensity may be notated as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, or \textit{f} depending on the local phrase, edition, and corpus convention. A model trained on MazurkaBL carries a learned expectation about how often each of these labels should occur, and this expectation can become wrong even when the metrical grid remains reasonably stable. The model is therefore learning an acoustic, metrical, and editorial mapping at the same time.
locations.before: This distinction explains several design choices. The model uses longer context because phrase-level dynamic intent extends beyond local note attacks. The post-processing snaps change points to beats because the available annotations are editorial and metrical rather than freely continuous. The evaluation is beat-synchronous because a musically meaningful score label should be judged on the score grid, not only on raw frame precision.
locations.after: Note-level velocity and score dynamics serve different purposes. Note-level velocity is the more precise target when the goal is editing or rendering, whereas beat-synchronous score dynamics is the more interpretable target when the goal is symbolic annotation, educational feedback, or performance analysis.

locations.quote: This chapter takes a different and simpler route. Instead of training on synthesised audio with synthetic labels, the front-end estimator is trained directly against real performance audio. The synthesiser is involved at training time only as a differentiable interface that connects predicted velocities to a measurable property of the real recording. This avoids the synthesis-to-performance domain gap that dominates synthetic-data transfer pipelines, at the cost of needing a differentiable supervision interface that is reliable across the instruments of interest.
locations.before:
\paragraph{Synthetic-data transfer for transcription.}
A common response to label scarcity in transcription is to train on synthesised audio, where symbolic labels are available by construction, and then transfer the model to real performances~\cite{maman2022general, zang2024synthtab, kusaka2025learn}. Recent works also use synthetic data and domain adaptation for annotation-free transcription and violin playing-technique recognition~\cite{sato2024annotationfree,wang2026vioptt}; these studies do not establish recovery of expressive note-level velocity on real non-piano recordings.
locations.after:
\paragraph{Differentiable waveform synthesisers.}
Differentiable digital signal processing provides a flexible route for embedding synthesis inside end-to-end learning~\cite{engel2020ddsp}. The same idea has been extended to MIDI-conditioned instrument synthesisers, including DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano} and the string-wise guitar model of Jonason~\emph{et~al.}~\cite{jonason2024guitar}. The original guitar model uses a loudness-derived proxy for MIDI velocity. In the Diff-Synth path studied here, the instrument-specific back-ends render predicted velocities into audio for adaptation with an audio reconstruction loss. The DDSP family also includes integrated systems with detailed expressive control~\cite{wu2022mididdsp}.

First, a Diff-Synth only approximates the real instrument; its waveform statistics differ from real recordings in timbre, articulation, microphone response, and room acoustics. locations.before:
\paragraph{Differentiable waveform synthesisers.}
Differentiable digital signal processing provides a flexible route for embedding synthesis inside end-to-end learning~\cite{engel2020ddsp}. The same idea has been extended to MIDI-conditioned instrument synthesisers, including DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano} and the string-wise guitar model of Jonason~\emph{et~al.}~\cite{jonason2024guitar}. The original guitar model uses a loudness-derived proxy for MIDI velocity. In the Diff-Synth path studied here, the instrument-specific back-ends render predicted velocities into audio for adaptation with an audio reconstruction loss. The DDSP family also includes integrated systems with detailed expressive control~\cite{wu2022mididdsp}.
locations.after:
\paragraph{Neural proxies for black-box audio systems.}
Because standard SoundFont rendering is non-differentiable, gradients cannot pass through it directly, which motivates a neural proxy. Mart\'inez Ram\'irez~\emph{et~al.}~\cite{martinez2021differentiable} demonstrated differentiable signal processing with black-box audio effects. Barkan~\emph{et~al.}~\cite{barkan2023is2} introduced InverSynth~II, which learns a differentiable synthesiser proxy for sound matching and combines it with self-supervised inference-time finetuning. Combes~\emph{et~al.}~\cite{combes2025neural} studied neural proxies that map presets to perceptually informed audio embeddings for black-box software synthesisers. Together, these approaches illustrate ways to incorporate non-differentiable audio processors into gradient-based optimisation.

locations.before: The combination of differentiable rendering and prediction networks defines an \emph{analysis-by-synthesis} setting. A network proposes control values for an observed recording; the renderer turns those values back into audio (or into an intermediate audio-derived quantity); a loss compares the rendered output with the observed signal. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} adopts the analysis-by-synthesis route explicitly under these constraints. proposals.text: The waveform interface supplies gradients through a differentiable approximation of the instrument. Its timbre and velocity response may differ from the target recordings. The observed degradation is consistent with this mismatch, but reconstruction fidelity and velocity-gradient accuracy were not measured separately on the target recordings.

Two limitations of waveform-level supervision are relevant here. First, a Diff-Synth only approximates the real instrument; its waveform statistics differ from real recordings in timbre, articulation, microphone response, and room acoustics. A waveform or spectral loss can be influenced by residual mismatch as well as velocity-dependent behaviour. Second, an instrument-specific Diff-Synth requires a dedicated design: piano-oriented synthesisers expect piano-specific controls such as pedal state, while guitar-oriented synthesisers expect string-wise trajectories. Reusing one Diff-Synth across instruments is therefore impractical.

Third, the asymmetry between the two adaptation interfaces widens with crop length. On FL dataset, Diff-Synth's $r_{\mathrm{BSSL}}$ falls by $0.083$ when moving from $2$\,s to $5$\,s, while Diff-SFProxy's $r_{\mathrm{BSSL}}$ varies within $0.01$. The crop-length pattern is consistent with greater exposure of the waveform objective to acoustic mismatch, but the present comparison does not isolate that mechanism.

Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy restricts the adapted control to velocity, but this does not remove effects of unobserved controls from the target audio. The recovered velocity may therefore absorb effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.

locations.quote: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.
locations.before: Chapter~\ref{ch:background} already introduced the ambiguity of score dynamics, the distinction between score dynamics and MIDI velocity, and the role of beats and downbeats as a musically meaningful coordinate. Rather than repeat that background, this chapter focuses on the concrete transcription problem studied in this work.
locations.after: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.

locations.quote: Third, score dynamics is inherently contextual. A dynamic marking is not a fixed loudness threshold. It depends on edition, local musical function, register, texture, and phrase context. Chapter~\ref{ch:audiodyn} treats score dynamics as a beat-synchronous symbolic target because that is the most useful interface for notation and analysis. The resulting labels should therefore be read as score-facing annotations under a specific annotation convention, not as universal statements about physical loudness.
locations.before: Second, the strongest direct supervision in the thesis remains piano-centric. This reflects the state of available velocity-labelled datasets rather than a belief that piano dynamics is the universal template for all instruments. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} addresses this bias by moving into a label-scarce guitar setting, but the broader point remains: once the target instrument lacks direct performance-control labels, the interpretation of recovered velocity must be stated operationally.
locations.after: Fourth, several chapters assume that structural coordinates are available or recoverable. Score-informed velocity correction assumes aligned score events. The beyond-piano proxy framework assumes aligned note events. Audio-to-score dynamics estimates beats and downbeats, but still relies on the idea that beat-synchronous output is the right symbolic interface. These assumptions are not weaknesses of the argument. They are the conditions under which label recovery, rather than unconstrained generation, becomes meaningful.

comments.original: The thesis has a clear central question: how musically interpretable dynamics labels can be recovered from incomplete, weakly expressive, or weakly supervised music data without changing note content or timing. This question gives the thesis a coherent intellectual framework and avoids the common problem of a PhD thesis appearing like a collection of disconnected papers. However, the thesis question is clearly articulated in the Abstract, Chapters 1 & 2, and revisited in the Conclusion. The technical chapters do address this question through speciﬁc recovery scenarios, such as symbolic velocity completion, score-informed velocity correction, audio-only score-dynamics recovery, and beyond-piano proxy-supervised velocity estimation. However, the connection between each technical chapter and the central thesis question could be made more explicit. I recommend a minor revision in which each technical chapter includes a short opening or closing paragraph that explains how that chapter addresses the central question under its speciﬁc data-availability condition. This is a minor revision, not a substantive ﬂaw. Technically, the contribution is substantial.

This question is studied under three core scenarios, outlined in Table~\ref{tab:intro_scenarios}. These scenarios represent a clear methodological progression. \textbf{Scenario S1} isolates the recovery task to a strict \textit{symbolic-only} setting. \textbf{Scenario S2} introduces acoustic evidence but maintains a reliable structural prior via an \textit{audio-plus-score} alignment. Finally, \textbf{Scenario S3} removes structural support entirely, tackling the fully open, \textit{audio-only} setting to recover a \textit{score-facing} target. By intentionally ordering these environments from the tightly constrained to the ambiguous, they form the core empirical arc of the thesis.

However, I think a clearer statement of which conclusions can and cannot be transferred to guitar, voice, bowed strings, and wind instruments would be more informative. This is a minor revision because the limitation is already acknowledged, but it could be improved.

locations.quote: Second, the strongest direct supervision in the thesis remains piano-centric. This reflects the state of available velocity-labelled datasets rather than a belief that piano dynamics is the universal template for all instruments. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} addresses this bias by moving into a label-scarce guitar setting, but the broader point remains: once the target instrument lacks direct performance-control labels, the interpretation of recovered velocity must be stated operationally.
locations.before: First, the thesis focuses on dynamics rather than on the full space of musical expression. Timing, articulation, pedalling, timbre, and phrasing interact with dynamics in real performance. The systems developed here isolate dynamics because it is perceptually salient, directly useful for data curation, and recoverable under structural preservation. This isolation is methodologically useful, but it also means that the recovered layer is one dimension of expression rather than a complete performance model.
locations.after: Third, score dynamics is inherently contextual. A dynamic marking is not a fixed loudness threshold. It depends on edition, local musical function, register, texture, and phrase context. Chapter~\ref{ch:audiodyn} treats score dynamics as a beat-synchronous symbolic target because that is the most useful interface for notation and analysis. The resulting labels should therefore be read as score-facing annotations under a specific annotation convention, not as universal statements about physical loudness.

locations.before:
\subsection{Instrument-general dynamics coordinates}
\label{ssec:conclusion:future_instruments}
locations.after: Future work can generalise the label-recovery stance by defining instrument-appropriate dynamics coordinates rather than forcing all instruments into piano-style velocity. For some instruments, the recovered layer may remain a MIDI-like note intensity value. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.

\paragraph{Score dynamics.}
Score dynamics represents the subjective cognitive intention of the composer or performer. Instead of attaching to isolated notes, markings like \textit{p} or \textit{crescendo} are conceptually anchored to the underlying metrical structure, acting as shared values across a specific beat or an entire phrase. This segment-level instruction provides a holistic perception of intensity while leaving room for free human interpretation. Because it is structurally aware and musically meaningful, score dynamics is the ideal target for pedagogical feedback and score analysis. In symbolic environments, the default assumption is often that missing score dynamics should be filled with \textit{mf} (mezzo-forte), which is the neutral middle ground of human perceptual loudness.

Dynamics is one of the most immediately audible dimensions of expressive performance. Listeners often perceive phrase direction, accent, and balance through intensity change before they perceive subtler aspects such as pedalling or micro-timing \cite{goebl2003role,cancinoChacon2018computational}. A transcription without dynamics therefore ignores a central part of musical meaning.

\paragraph{Symbolic editability.}
locations.after:
\paragraph{Data scalability.}
Many expressive targets, particularly in the Control Layer, depend on fine-grained, instrument-specific mechanisms. Although recent datasets have begun to capture control parameters, such parameters remain sparse and weakly standardised \cite{ryu2024midfild,lee2025gigamidi,tamer2023violin,loth2025goat,xie2025finegrained} across different instruments. By contrast, dynamics has already proved tractable across several practical paradigms, including piano and singing-voice dynamics estimation \cite{kim2024method,narang2024automatic}. It thus provides a scalable entry point for expressive AMT, bypassing the bottleneck of instrument-specific data scarcity.

Score dynamics is also a core pedagogical dimension. In automatic piano performance assessment, dynamics is routinely treated alongside pitch, timing, and rhythm as one of the salient components of performance quality and feedback \cite{kim2022piano}. More recent work on query-based music coaching likewise emphasises that useful educational feedback needs interpretable information about expressive shaping, not only note correctness \cite{zhang2025llaqo,park2025dynvisual}. In many educational scenarios, a reference score is already available together with a student performance audio. This makes score-informed dynamics estimation especially attractive, because the symbolic prior can stabilise the prediction while keeping the feedback musically meaningful.

locations.before:
This section identifies a narrower and more practical research gap than the general claim that AMT still lacks expressiveness. A recurring paradox in music research is that while structural data (pitch and timing) is increasingly abundant, expressive data remains systematically impoverished. A MIDI file may contain correct note sequences while leaving all velocities at a default constant. A performance corpus may preserve audio and aligned scores but only sparse, unreliable, or absent dynamic markings. The common problem is therefore how to recover a missing expressive label layer from data that are already partly specified.

\paragraph{The ontological gap: dynamics must be inferred across representations.}
locations.after:
\paragraph{The ambiguity of ground truth: dynamics is more fragile than notes.}
For note transcription, pitch and onset often remain learnable under moderate changes in instrument, room, or recording conditions. Dynamics ground truth is less stable. Small changes in instruments (timbre), microphone placement, editorial convention, or synthesis setup can alter the apparent relation between sound, MIDI velocity, and score dynamics notation. For non-piano settings, the difficulty becomes sharper because the bottleneck is not ordinary domain shift but missing measurement itself: reliable MIDI velocity labels are rarely available, and in some cases even the ground truth is instrument-dependent.

\begin{abstract}
	Automatic music transcription has matured in its treatment of note pitch and timing, but musical dynamics remains less fully addressed. This thesis treats dynamics as a missing expressive label layer that can be recovered from music data already partly specified, without rewriting note content or note timing. Its unifying question is \emph{how musically interpretable dynamics labels can be recovered from incomplete, weakly expressive, or weakly supervised music data}. Two complementary targets within expressive music performance recur throughout: note-level MIDI velocity, the per-onset control variable used in MIDI workflows, and score-level dynamics, the beat-aligned markings such as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, and \textit{f} written in notation.
locations.after: It then turns to score-informed velocity estimation in the audio-plus-score setting, using a Transformer correction module that refines AMT-estimated velocity at aligned score onsets. Rather than replacing the AMT backbone, the module uses score structure as a late correction prior, transfers across the HPT, HPPNet, and DynEst backbones, improves cross-dataset behaviour from MAESTRO to SMD, and remains stable under audio--score timing shifts of up to several seconds.

The 30-second setting is included because it is a common choice in beat/downbeat tracking systems, including Beat This \cite{foscarin2024beat}. locations.before: The combination of differentiable rendering and prediction networks defines an \emph{analysis-by-synthesis} setting. A network proposes control values for an observed recording; the renderer turns those values back into audio (or into an intermediate audio-derived quantity); a loss compares the rendered output with the observed signal. This paradigm becomes the central tool when true note-level velocity labels are unavailable, because the renderer takes the place of a label by linking predicted control to a measurable property of the recording.
locations.after: For expressive AMT, this strategy is attractive but delicate. It makes label-scarce learning possible, yet it also ties the learning signal to the adequacy of the renderer: a proxy objective can reward compatibility with the synthesiser more than compatibility with real instrumental control, and reconstruction error is therefore not the same thing as accurate velocity recovery. Chapter~\ref{ch:beyondpiano} adopts the analysis-by-synthesis route explicitly under these constraints. It contrasts a waveform-domain DDSP-style supervision interface with a low-dimensional parameter-space proxy built from a frozen SoundFont teacher, and treats proxy supervision as a method family with explicit limits rather than as a universal substitute for true note-level labels.

Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
